Unlabelled

Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping clinical research, diagnostics, health system operations, and medical education. Frontier generative AI development is increasingly concentrated in private industry, whose computational infrastructure, proprietary datasets, and capital exceed those of most academic institutions. Although not designed exclusively for medicine, these systems increasingly influence clinical applications. This shift raises a question for academic medical centers (AMCs): What role remains when leading AI systems emerge outside universities? This viewpoint examines industry's growing role in generative AI, clarifies AMCs' responsibilities, and proposes a framework for AI governance and literacy across undergraduate, graduate, and continuing medical education (CME). Rather than compete with industry on computational scale, AMCs should reinforce functions for which AMCs have distinctive strengths. These include (1) mechanistic inquiry linking algorithmic outputs to biological and pathophysiologic understanding; (2) interdisciplinary synthesis integrating clinical, ethical, legal, and sociotechnical perspectives; (3) independent and methodologically rigorous validation of clinical AI tools; and (4) institutional stewardship of ethical governance for patient populations that are often underrepresented in commercial datasets. As nonprofit institutions training clinicians, AMCs have a distinct role in safeguarding transparency, fairness, and accountability in AI-enabled health care. We position this 4-role framework to refine AI governance and translational medicine approaches, clarifying which responsibilities AMCs should retain while collaborating with industry. The approach includes longitudinal AI literacy training across undergraduate medical education, graduate medical education, and CME, standardized pathways for evaluating clinical AI, stronger conflict-of-interest safeguards, and complementary partnerships with industry and regulators. We also outline educational assessment methods and safety-monitoring processes, including competency-based assessment across undergraduate medical education, graduate medical education, and CME, postdeployment monitoring, and clear escalation triggers. Embedding verification habits and governance into training and practice can help ensure that generative AI supports clinical reasoning while preserving trust, equity, and scientific rigor. This viewpoint addresses academic leaders, curriculum committees, residency directors, faculty developers, and accreditors. Safe clinical AI requires sustained academic leadership.\", \"doi\": \"10.2196/89741\", \"pmid\": \"42896100\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13679860\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.2196/89741\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13679860\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13679860?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"A strategic pathway for the ethical development of AI tools in dementia care.\", \"abstract\": \"Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering dementia clinical practice, offering opportunities across the care continuum. However, cognitive decline creates a unique ethical challenge. This perspective article proposes a strategy to ensure the responsible development and deployment of AI tools for dementia. An interdisciplinary workgroup of the Alzheimer's Association Innovation Roundtable synthesized ethical frameworks, regulatory standards, and empirical evidence to generate expert consensus. The result is a six-step strategic pathway tailored to dementia care: establish ethical foundations, conduct stakeholder engagement, lead a co-design approach, conduct an impact assessment, establish iterative design and feedback loops, and provide education and digital literacy. A practical implementation checklist accompanies the framework. Because responsible progress requires both safety and timely innovation, ethical evaluation must balance the risks of premature deployment against those of harmful delay. Operationalizing ethics throughout the AI lifecycle can ensure that innovation advances autonomy, equity, and safety for people living with dementia.\", \"doi\": \"10.1002/alz.71805\", \"pmid\": \"42675027\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13529824\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1002/alz.71805\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13529824\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13529824?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"High-risk without safeguards? The EU AI Act and the push for deregulation of medical AI.\", \"abstract\": \"Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in clinical decision-making, yet recent proposals to simplify the European Union (EU) Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) have reopened the question of whether AI-enabled medical devices should remain subject to the AI Act's full high-risk regime. Under the current framework, AI-enabled medical devices are regulated through a combination of sectoral medical device legislation (the Medical Devices Regulation (MDR) and In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation (IVDR)) and additional AI-specific safeguards contained in the AI Act. This narrative review analyses the Health Innovation Package and related legislative developments under the EU simplification agenda and examines their impact on the relationship between the AI Act and medical device law. It shows that the proposed reform would retain the high-risk classification of AI-enabled medical devices while removing most associated AI Act obligations. In effect, this decouples risk classification from the safeguards that give it regulatory meaning, including requirements on data governance, risk management, human oversight and postmarket monitoring. Rather than resolving regulatory overlap, the amendments shift the centre of gravity back to product-focused medical device law without ensuring equivalent AI-specific safeguards. These changes may narrow attention to fundamental rights, weaken oversight in clinical use and increase legal uncertainty regarding accountability and responsibility. In a domain where AI systems directly shape clinical decisions and patient outcomes, these changes risk undermining the conditions for safe, equitable and accountable deployment of medical AI.\", \"doi\": \"10.1136/bmjdh-2026-000184\", \"pmid\": \"42825232\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13629938\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjdh-2026-000184\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13629938\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13629938?pdf=render\"}]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "f71c742f406d9b1aa7573d202619049866e0400ca5430d79aa8c8eb5efeff021", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "responsibility_formation", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2196/89741", "doi:10.1002/alz.71805", "doi:10.1136/bmjdh-2026-000184", "pmc:PMC13642710", "pmc:PMC13679860", "pmc:PMC13529824", "pmc:PMC13629938"], "source_candidates": ["https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13642710/?tool=EBI", "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13642710/pdf/?tool=EBI", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13642710", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13642710?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.2196/89741", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13679860", "https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13679860?pdf=render", "https://doi.org/10.1002/alz.71805"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
